items.title: Chip stocks had their worst day since the summer after Lam Research warned of supply constraints
items.summary: On Thursday 22 October the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 6.72 percent to 10,731.98. That was its weakest session since the summer and its lowest close since 29 July. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.6 percent to 26,008.86, its worst day since early June. Lam Research fell about 11.8 percent, Applied Materials about 8.2 percent, AMD about 8.1 percent, Marvell about 8 percent, Intel about 7 percent and Nvidia 4.4 percent (to 212.21 dollars). The trigger was Lam Research's earnings call on 21 October. CFO Doug Bettinger said the revenue guidance would have been higher without near-term supply chain constraints. CEO Tim Archer said cleanroom space and component shortages would limit chipmakers into 2027. Worries about Meta's spending and about how AI expansion will be financed also weighed. Chip stocks recovered only partly on Friday 23 October.
items.why_it_matters: A warning about supply bottlenecks at an equipment maker combined with fears over how AI is financed to wipe out a large amount of chip-sector value in one day. Investors are now punishing both supply constraints and high capex.

items.title: Meta raises the floor of its AI investment guidance, reports negative free cash flow and the stock falls 7 percent
items.summary: Meta reported third-quarter revenue of 64.6 billion dollars, up 26 percent and above the expected 63.3 billion. Capex was 34.9 billion dollars, against 19.4 billion a year earlier. Full-year 2026 capex guidance was narrowed to 135-145 billion dollars, from 130-145 billion. Free cash flow was negative 2.1 billion dollars. Operating profit was pulled down by a settlement of about 10 billion dollars over youth safety. Meta also plans to create a new non-voting class C share, among other things to fund the AI build-out. The stock fell about 7 percent on 22 October, and the spread on Meta's five-year credit default swaps reached a record high.
items.why_it_matters: The first big-tech company to report negative free cash flow because of AI investment. Higher credit risk and a new share class show that the build-out is now being financed with debt and equity, not just cash flow.

items.title: OpenAI lowers its valuation to 1.25 trillion dollars in a new funding round of up to 30 billion
items.summary: According to Bloomberg, OpenAI is raising up to 30 billion dollars at a pre-money valuation of 1.25 trillion dollars. That is about 150 billion below the 1.4 trillion it presented to investors earlier in October. If the full amount comes in, the post-money valuation would be about 1.28 trillion dollars. The round is reportedly led by investors from the UAE and by Coatue, and OpenAI wants agreements signed by the end of the following week. The round is described as a bridge to a future IPO. The terms are not final.
items.why_it_matters: A downward adjustment of the price for the world's most valuable private AI company is a clear sign that investors are tightening terms after weaker revenue figures and the market turmoil.

items.title: OpenAI's models launch on Google Cloud and are now on all three major US cloud platforms
items.summary: On Wednesday 21 October OpenAI and Google Cloud announced that OpenAI's models and Codex workflows will be available in Google Cloud's Model Garden, initially as a private preview. Customers can buy through Google Cloud Marketplace and draw down existing spending commitments with Google. The models are later expected in Google Antigravity and Gemini Agent. Microsoft's exclusivity ended in April 2026, when OpenAI also launched on AWS. Google is the last of the three major US hyperscalers to offer OpenAI's models.
items.why_it_matters: Companies can now choose models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic within the same cloud platform. That weakens Microsoft's special position and makes the model layer more of a commodity.

items.title: Salesforce buys Braze for 5.66 billion dollars to strengthen AI-driven marketing
items.summary: On 20 October Salesforce agreed to buy the customer engagement platform Braze for about 5.66 billion dollars in enterprise value. It is paying 47.50 dollars per share in cash, a premium of about 58 percent over the previous closing price, and Braze shares rose more than 50 percent. Braze uses AI for personalised messages and real-time responses to customer behaviour. The deal is expected to close in Salesforce's fiscal year 2028, and the termination fees are 300 million dollars for Salesforce and 191.4 million for Braze.
items.why_it_matters: A sign that established software companies are buying their way to AI capabilities as investors worry that AI agents will undermine the traditional SaaS model.

items.title: SpaceX and Tesla set up board committees to assess a possible merger
items.summary: On SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call on 20 October, Elon Musk said the boards of SpaceX and Tesla have each set up special committees of independent directors to assess a possible merger. Musk said he is a conflicted party and is not taking part in the talks. No terms have been agreed. A deal would require support from 50 percent of all Tesla shareholders. Among Musk's arguments are cooperation on AI software, robotics, the orbital data centre project Starmind and the joint chip factory Terafab. SpaceX's 10-Q filing states that there is no guarantee of an agreement.
items.why_it_matters: A combination of SpaceX (which includes xAI) and Tesla would create one of the world's largest AI and robotics groups. It also raises major questions about corporate governance and minority shareholders.

items.title: IBM fell 7 percent after its CEO warned of AI spending without real returns
items.summary: IBM reported third-quarter revenue of 17.1 billion dollars and adjusted earnings per share of 2.95 dollars on 21 October, both above expectations. It kept its growth forecast of 4-5 percent at constant currency. On the earnings call, CEO Arvind Krishna said customers are increasingly scrutinising the real return on AI investments, and warned of 'some of the AI spending completely out of control with no real return'. The stock fell about 7 percent to 233.50 dollars on 22 October, and Accenture and Infosys also fell.
items.why_it_matters: A major enterprise supplier says openly that customers are demanding ROI from AI. That is highly relevant to consulting firms and to the debate over whether the AI investments will pay off.

items.title: Nvidia commits nearly 10 billion dollars to Europe and launches prefabricated data centre modules at GTC Berlin
items.summary: At GTC Berlin on 21 October Jensen Huang said Nvidia has committed nearly 10 billion dollars to the European technology ecosystem. He presented DSX POD, factory-built data centre modules based on Vera Rubin that Nvidia says can be deployed in about two weeks instead of six months. Nvidia also announced partnerships with European industrial companies and startups, and a joint declaration of intent with the German government. German Agile Robots plans to produce 1,000-2,000 humanoid robots with Nvidia next year. On the same day Nvidia announced capacity expansions with six suppliers, including SPIL and Unimicron.
items.why_it_matters: Europe is courted as the next market for AI infrastructure, and much faster data centre construction could change the economics of projects in the Nordics too.

items.title: Anthropic in talks with Nscale on a second computing deal worth about 45 billion dollars
items.summary: According to Bloomberg and Reuters on 19 October, Nvidia-backed Nscale is negotiating a new deal worth about 45 billion dollars with Anthropic. The deal would cover a second building at the Monarch campus in West Virginia, delivering 460 MW with Nvidia Vera Rubin chips. Anthropic has a right of first refusal on a planned third building. In August Anthropic agreed to rent computing power worth 45 billion dollars from the same campus. Nscale's total contracted value has grown to more than 103 billion dollars. The talks are not final.
items.why_it_matters: Shows how quickly Anthropic is buying computing power ahead of its planned IPO, and how dependent neocloud players like Nscale are on a few major customers.

items.title: Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises 1 billion dollars at a 6 billion valuation
items.summary: Flapping Airplanes announced a Series A of 1 billion dollars co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a valuation of 6 billion dollars. Nine months ago a seed round of 180 million valued the company at 1.5 billion. Sequoia, GV and Kleiner Perkins took part, and Nvidia is among its investors. The company is building models that need less training data and are cheaper to train and run. On 20 October Bloomberg also reported that the Boston company ASI (formerly Air Space Intelligence) raised 325 million dollars at a 3 billion valuation in a round led by Spark Capital.
items.why_it_matters: Even amid the market turmoil, venture investors pay billion-dollar valuations for young labs that promise cheaper and more data-efficient AI.

items.title: Trump says new data centres must produce their own power and pay a 'dividend' to local communities
items.summary: In a Truth Social post on 21 October, President Donald Trump wrote that large new data centres are 'mandated' to generate their own electricity, deliver surplus power to the community or grid, and pay a 'dividend' to local communities. The post gave no amounts, no enforcement mechanism and no federal programme, and it is unclear whether an executive order will follow. Earlier in October the federal energy regulator FERC rejected attempts to require data centres to bring their own generation to the largest US grid.
items.why_it_matters: Local opposition and electricity prices have become a political issue ahead of the midterm elections, which could raise costs and slow the timeline for American AI data centres.
